metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: Course pitch redo, not a channel explainer. The instructor's feedback asked for the problem to be shown first, so B01 is a narrated title card (project title + Riya's name + the problem) and B02 shows the problem with a real example, replacing the hesitant writer and the terms card (SQL is defined in the narration where it is first used). No Your Turn (a pitch has no viewer task). No ClaudeTitleOutro: it hardcodes the instructor's handle, which the assignment forbids; the film ends on its spoken conclusion B20.
metadata.audience: INFO 7375 instructor and TAs; a hiring manager screening AI Engineer candidates; anyone who uses AI to ask a database questions

beats.narration_text: Picture an analyst asking an AI: what is our revenue by country? The AI writes SQL, the language for asking a database questions. It runs. No errors. It says the USA made four thousand six hundred sixty seven dollars. The real answer is five hundred twenty three.

beats.narration_text: Why does this matter? People ask data questions in plain English, so most never see the SQL. The AI doesn't know your data. And wrong SQL doesn't crash. It just gives a number people trust, and that number ends up in reports and decisions.

beats.narration_text: So I'm building Ground Truth SQL: a test for AI data assistants. Give it your own data and questions, and it tells you which answers the AI got wrong, and why.

beats.narration_text: Where will it be used? Anywhere people ask data questions in plain English: store sales, finance, hospitals, marketing, and AI data assistants. Analysts learn what to double check. Teams test a tool before buying. Engineers see what to fix.

beats.narration_text: Others have tested AI on SQL. BIRD is a public benchmark: twelve thousand seven hundred fifty one questions over ninety five databases, scored by checking results. People score about ninety three percent, and the best AI still scores lower. But BIRD tests AI only on its own databases, not yours.

beats.narration_text: Tools like Vanna write SQL on your own data, and come with a built-in answer test. But that test looks for words, not right numbers. On my data, it passed the answer that was nine times too high.

beats.narration_text: So there's a gap. Benchmarks check numbers, but not on your data. Tools work on your data, but don't check the numbers. Ground Truth SQL does both, so you find the wrong answers before anyone trusts them.

beats.narration_text: It worked if the checker agrees with my hand labels every time, every answer key passes the second check, and every miss on the report card has a named cause. It didn't work if Claude gets everything right, because that means my questions are too easy. Today it nearly does, so the next fifty questions must be harder.

beats.narration_text: In conclusion: AI can give wrong answers that look right. Ground Truth SQL tests the AI on your own data and shows what's wrong, and why. Today the checker works. Next: fifty harder questions. So the takeaway is this: running SQL is easy. Being right is the test.
